Reproductive investment in Small yellow croaker (Larimichthys polyactis) varies markedly with local thermal conditions. During a survey conducted in the East China Sea at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 12% [GSI = 12%] during the pre-spawning aggregation period. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs at a total length of 0.46 centimeters [Lb = 0.46 centimeters], a diminutive size that reflects the relatively small diameter of the yolk-laden egg from which they hatch. This initial length is consistent with the typical dimensions observed among other sciaenid larvae at the onset of the yolk-sac larval stage, a critical period during which the developing fish relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding.

Longitudinal growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis reveal that individuals reach their ultimate total length at approximately 40 centimeters [Li = approximately 40 centimeters], a value that corresponds closely with the asymptotic size reported in earlier fishery-independent surveys for this species across its range in the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea. Sexual maturation is initiated considerably earlier, as the total length at puberty has been measured at 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a threshold that many individuals attain during their first or second growing season. This marked disparity between the length at which reproductive competence is achieved and the ultimate body size attainable suggests an early onset of reproductive activity, a life-history strategy that may confer resilience under fluctuating fishing pressure.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to simulate the thermal regime of the Yellow Sea during the spring spawning window, the daily egg production rate was assessed. At a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], reproductively active females exhibited a maximum fecundity of approximately 575 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 575 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season. When this daily output is combined with field observations indicating that individual females sustain such spawning activity every day throughout the protracted spawning period, the resulting total reproductive effort underscores the species’ considerable capacity for population renewal. This elevated fecundity is typical of small-bodied, iteroparous sciaenids that inhabit productive coastal ecosystems.

The transition from the pelagic larval phase to the demersal juvenile stage is accompanied by a series of critical physiological milestones. At a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the embryonation period lasts approximately 6.1 days [ab = approximately 6.1 days], after which the emerging yolk-sac larva weighs a mere 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value derived from the geometric volume of the spherical egg capsule. By the time individuals achieve the total length at puberty of 7 centimeters, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been observed to reach 5.4 grams [Wwp = 5.4 grams]. This dramatic increase in somatic mass over the intervening growth period reflects the rapid accumulation of muscle tissue and skeletal structure during the juvenile and sub-adult phases.

Comparative life-history analyses indicate that the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals, based on otolith annulus counts, reaches approximately 8,395 days [am = approximately 8,395 days] under thermal conditions averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Within this extended lifespan, the time since birth at puberty for male and female croaker alike has been estimated at 250 days after birth [tp = 250 days after birth] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a relatively brief juvenile period that enables first spawning to occur within the first year of life. Adults that survive to attain the ultimate wet weight of 1,011 grams [Wwi = 1,011 grams] have often been aged at over a decade, illustrating the species’ capacity for sustained somatic growth well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. This long reproductive window, combined with early maturation, underpins the population dynamics of this commercially important sciaenid.
